summary.text: A nova is a sudden flare in which a bright, apparently new star appears and then fades slowly over weeks or months.
Every observed nova involves a white dwarf in a close binary system, which draws gas from its companion until that gas ignites in runaway fusion.
The sudden energy expels the gas layer into space, creating the glowing envelope seen as the nova.

facts.label: How often
facts.value: About ten per year in the Milky Way

facts.label: Repeat example
facts.value: RS Ophiuchi flared seven times, most recently in 2021

items.prompt: A bright "new star" appears in the sky and fades over months. What is actually happening there?

options.label: A very old stellar remnant in a close pair has ignited gas taken from its partner
A brand-new star is forming out of a collapsing gas cloud
A distant galaxy has just drifted into view
A lone star has swelled into a giant

items.explain: Novae most often take place on white dwarfs, remnants of extremely old stars, in close binaries that feed the white dwarf matter.

items.prompt: Heated gas usually expands and cools. Why does hydrogen piled on a white dwarf ignite in a runaway instead?

options.label: The companion star keeps cooling the layer down
The star's magnetic field squeezes the hydrogen
The star's fast rotation keeps the gas from leaving
The dense star's matter stops the gas from expanding as it heats

items.explain: The white dwarf is degenerate matter, so the accreted hydrogen cannot expand even as its temperature rises, until runaway fusion starts at about 20 million K.

items.prompt: RS Ophiuchi has flared seven times since 1898. What lets a nova repeat?

options.label: The white dwarf slowly regrows fuel from fusion in its core
Its companion keeps feeding the dense atmosphere after each ignition
Gas ejected by the first flare falls back onto it
A second white dwarf merges with it each time

items.explain: A recurrent nova repeats because the companion star again feeds the white dwarf's dense atmosphere after each ignition.

items.prompt: Hydrogen piles onto a compact star in a pair and ignites. What makes the result a Type Ia supernova rather than a nova?

options.label: The companion star runs out of hydrogen first
The outburst fades more slowly than 80 days
The fusion wrecks the star itself instead of only throwing off its outer gas
The ejected gas moves faster than several thousand km/s

items.explain: If accretion triggers runaway fusion that destroys the white dwarf rather than merely expelling its atmosphere, the event is usually classified as a Type Ia supernova.

items.prompt: Tycho Brahe's "new star" of 1572 later proved to be a supernova. How did astronomers treat the words nova and supernova until then?

options.label: As interchangeable terms, until the 1930s
As distinct, since novae were always dimmer
As distinct, set apart by Brahe himself
As interchangeable only for stars seen to repeat

items.explain: SN 1572 was later found to be a supernova, but the terms were considered interchangeable until the 1930s.

items.prompt: Two novae both reach peak brightness. What is used to sort them into fast and slow?

options.label: How far each lies from the Milky Way's center
How long each takes to fade by a few magnitudes from maximum
How bright each is at its peak
How many times each has flared before

items.explain: The time taken to decay by 2 or 3 magnitudes from maximum optical brightness groups novae into speed classes.
